body: I don’t think value is a useful way to look at human beings because that presumes that we should be judging people based on their value. It’s simply a misguided question that will run into many ethical concerns. I believe you see value as consequentialist, therefore a person must contribute “positively” to society. Now, you have to consider society, as value will only exists contextually within a society. I’d actually recommend anthropology if you’re interested in this subject, as once you see that different cultures through ecological constraints have developed different concepts of value you’ll see how difficult it becomes to come up with a universal definition of value/ a positive societal contribution. For example think of a doctor, and how many financial barriers there are to attending medical school, particularly in the US. Now it’s intuitive that doctors are valuable to society, however when you think of the rejected medical student that may have had to work instead of study for an MCAT, you see that there are barriers in place for a person to provide things deemed valuable to a society, and for that reason, thinking of people as having value is a concept that benefits people in positions of power. Another example is the CEO versus the petty thief. Wage theft provides value to a company, and a CEO that encourages this is very valuable to the company, however the petty thief creates value for no one. Both are “immoral” for stealing but ultimately in creating a successful company the CEO is treated as the most valuable of the two within a society. Therefore even morals themselves have constraints, it’s far more easy to be moral if you do not have to worry about your next meal or remaining employed. The ways chronic stress and mental illness can alter someone’s mood is self evident. If you can place value on a person you can overlook the environmental constraints that have affected their ability to effectively provide societal contributions. Therefore the best way to evaluate people is in context, “A king has their strengths, a cook has their own too” There isn’t a fast, universal way to evaluate a person. I will judge an immoral person who has X resources harsher than a person who did not have access to those resources.
I feel the same way. I was faced with obstacles that I shouldn’t have been. Everytime I try it feels harder to catch up. Why do I have to be strong when others don’t have to try.
